# System Design and Wiring

Status: **proposal, 2026-11-03**. Based on the 3D scratch design (heaters on
the back wall, divider in the middle, four PT100s, HV in from the side, three
readouts on the other side), the meeting notes, and
[`HEATER_AND_CURRENT_DRIVER.md`](HEATER_AND_CURRENT_DRIVER.md).

The step-by-step task list is in [`../TODO.md`](../TODO.md). Parts are in
[`../ORDER_LIST.md`](../ORDER_LIST.md). Software installation and commissioning
are in [`../HOW_TO_RUN.md`](../HOW_TO_RUN.md), Part B.

## 1. Short answers

### Is the 3D design compatible with the suggested parts?

Yes, with four adjustments:

1. **Heater wall parallel to the board stack.** Keep the heaters on the back
   wall, spread along the full length of the stack, as drawn. Then every board
   is the same distance from the heat source. The unavoidable gradient runs
   front-to-back, the same for all boards, not along the divider from the HV
   end to the LV end. A gradient along the divider is what shifts the ratio.
   Do not put the heaters at either end of the stack.
2. **Insulation outside the box.** This matches the July notes ("Insulate the
   walls. Foam installation outside."). An external foam jacket keeps foam
   away from the HV region and costs no clearance. The whole aluminum shell
   then sits inside the thermal envelope and acts as a uniform-temperature
   enclosure around the divider.
3. **PT100 readout electronics outside.** The sketch shows a "PT100 readouts"
   block inside the box. Move the four MAX31865 boards to the controller box
   with the Pi. Only the passive 4-wire sensor leads enter the divider box. A
   4-wire measurement is insensitive to lead length, and no SPI clock or
   digital electronics are left next to the divider.
4. **Heater-plate sensor needs its own trip limit.** A sensor on the heater
   plate normally runs several kelvin above the air: roughly 5–10 K at the
   ~5 W steady state, more during warm-up. The current code trips every
   monitor sensor at 31 °C, so this sensor would shut the heater off. This is
   a small software change, TODO **S1**. Until then, use the interim setting
   in [section 8](#8-software-mapping-for-this-layout).

The Phase-1 resistors and the Phase-2 Kapton heater both mount on an aluminum
spreader plate on the back wall. The linear current driver, 24 V supply and Pi
sit outside, as you described.

### Why DC heater power?

Heating itself does not care: `P = I²R` gives the same heat from AC or DC.
DC was chosen because of everything else the heater current does:

| Reason | AC mains heater (e.g. 120 VAC) | DC from a linear driver |
|---|---|---|
| **Electric-field pickup** | Heater wires swing ±170 V at 60 Hz. Even 1 pF of stray capacitance to a divider node injects `2π·60 Hz·1 pF·120 V ≈ 45 nA`, which is ~45 mV across 1 MΩ. The divider is full of high-impedance nodes. | Voltage is constant, so `i = C·dV/dt = 0`. No injected current. |
| **Magnetic pickup** | 60 Hz current induces voltage in any nearby loop (∝ dI/dt). | Static current, so no induced voltage. |
| **Continuous control** | Practical mains controllers switch: relay, SSR, burst or phase firing. That gives on/off heat and switching spikes. | Current can be set to any value and held constant. |
| **Safety inside an HV box** | Mains wiring, mains insulation and protective-earth rules inside the HV enclosure. | Everything inside stays below 50 V, as stated in the July notes ("Keep everything below 50 V inside"). |

DC is **necessary but not sufficient**. A DC supply that switches (LED drivers,
PWM, buck converters) brings back fast dV/dt and dI/dt at kHz–MHz. That is why
the driver is linear.

This also rules out aquarium heaters. They are mains-voltage and contain their
own bimetal on/off thermostat.

### Continuous, not bang-bang

There are three ways a controller can deliver its output:

| Style | What the heater sees | Example |
|---|---|---|
| On/off ("bang-bang") | Full power or zero, switched at the setpoint | Simple thermostat, aquarium heater |
| Time-proportioning PID | Full power or zero, with the **duty cycle** set by PID (e.g. 30 % = on 3 s of every 10 s) | Panel PID controllers with relay or SSR outputs |
| **Continuous (analog) PID** | A steady current whose **value** is set by PID | **This design**; panel controllers with an analog output option |

In this design nothing ever switches the heater on and off during regulation:

- The PID updates every 1 s.
- The current is slew-limited to ≤0.05 A/s.
- The DAC step is 0.32 mA and is smoothed by a 60 ms filter.
- The linear driver holds the current at that value continuously.

The relay closes once at start-up and opens only on a fault or a stop.

### The Omega controllers

The Omega/DwyerOmega Platinum (CNPT) controllers do run a real PID algorithm.
They look bang-bang because of their **output stage**:

- Relay or SSR outputs can only switch, so the PID result becomes on/off time
  proportioning. The CN8PT-330, for example, has two relay outputs and no
  analog output.
- Some CNPT variants have an **analog (voltage/current) output**. That version
  driving this same linear driver would be continuous. They accept 2-, 3- or
  4-wire Pt100 inputs.

The Pi is still the better fit here:

- it reads and logs all four sensors and the heater current;
- it implements the sensor-fault and gradient checks;
- it drives the display;
- it costs far less. The CN8PT-330 was listed at $521 with a long lead time.

An analog-output Omega controller is a reasonable independent backup, not a
requirement.

### What is SCPI?

SCPI ("Standard Commands for Programmable Instruments") is just the text
command language that lab instruments understand over LAN or USB, for example
`CH1:CURRent 0.5`.

The software has two interchangeable ways to output the heater current:

| `hardware.mode` | Current source | When |
|---|---|---|
| **`"dac"`** | Pi → MCP4725 DAC → **our linear driver** → heater | **The final design. Use this.** |
| `"scpi"` | Pi → LAN → programmable bench power supply → heater | Only to start thermal tests before the driver is built, or as an A/B reference during noise tests |

If we are not buying a bench supply, ignore SCPI entirely. Nothing else in the
design depends on it.

## 2. Architecture

```text
 OUTSIDE: controller box (all electronics)                    INSIDE: divider enclosure (insulated jacket outside)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ CB-PWR 24 V ─F1 3 A─┬─ DC-DC 24→5 V (isolated) ─ Pi  │     │  back wall: Al spreader plate                     │
│                     ├─ driver board (+12 V reg)      │     │    TF1 72 °C ─ TS1 49 °C ─ H1 ─ H2  (series)      │
│                     └─F2 1.6 A─ relay K1 ─ INA260 ───┼─────┼─► DB-HTR ──────────────────────────────┐         │
│ driver Q1 drain ◄────────────────────────────────────┼─────┼── DB-HTR ◄─────────────────────────────┘         │
│                                                      │     │                                                   │
│ Pi ─SPI─ 4× MAX31865 ◄───────────────────────────────┼─────┼── DB-RTD1  S1 air, control (PID)                  │
│                      ◄───────────────────────────────┼─────┼── DB-RTD2  S2 air, far side (monitor)             │
│                      ◄───────────────────────────────┼─────┼── DB-RTD3  S3 ground (LV) board                   │
│                      ◄───────────────────────────────┼─────┼── DB-RTD4  S4 heater plate                        │
│ Pi ─I²C─ MCP4725 DAC ─0–3.3 V─► driver CMD           │     │                                                   │
│ Pi ─I²C─ INA260, LCD (via level shifter)             │     │  divider stack, centered, parallel to back wall   │
│ Pi ─GPIO17─ relay K1                                 │     │  HV in (one side) · 3 readouts (other side)       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Only two kinds of conductors cross into the divider box:

- the DC heater pair;
- the four passive PT100 cables.

### Signal chain, one loop iteration (every 1 s)

1. Each MAX31865 measures its PT100 resistance (4-wire) and returns a digital
   value to the Pi over SPI.
2. The Pi converts the reading to °C, applies the calibration, checks for
   faults and limits, and runs PI on S1.
3. The PI output is a requested power P. The Pi converts it to current with
   `I = √(P/R)`, then applies the limits and slew.
4. The Pi writes a 12-bit code to the MCP4725 over I²C. The DAC outputs
   `V_DAC = 0–3.3 V`.
5. The driver scales it to `V_A = 0.4·V_DAC` and forces `I_heater = V_A / 1 Ω`
   with a linear MOSFET loop.
6. The INA260 measures the real current and voltage. The Pi logs them and
   shows them on the LCD.

## 3. Inside the divider enclosure

### Layout

- **Board stack:** centered front-to-back and parallel to the back wall (long
  axis left-right, as drawn). HV in on the left, readouts on the right.
- **Heater zone:** one aluminum spreader plate covering most of the back wall
  behind the stack.
  - Phase 1: H1 and H2 (10 Ω each, in series) at about ¼ and ¾ of the stack
    length.
  - Phase 2: Kapton strip(s) along the same span.
  - TS1 (thermostat) and TF1 (thermal fuse) are clamped to the plate next to
    the heaters.
- **Sensors:**

| ID | Software channel | Where | Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | `control_air` (PID input) | Air, mid-height, between the heater wall and the stack (about ⅓ of the gap from the stack), at mid-length. Optionally shield its heater-facing side with a small piece of polished Al so it reads air, not radiation. | 1/8" probe |
| S2 | `monitor_air` | Air on the **front** side of the stack (or near the HV-in end), mid-height. Measures the gradient across the divider. This is the "spare" from the sketch, given a useful job. | 1/8" probe |
| S3 | `ground_board` | Surface of the **ground (LV) board only**. Never on a board at HV potential. | Surface PT100 |
| S4 | `spare` (heater plate; see S1 in TODO) | Spreader plate, between H1 and H2 | Surface PT100 |

- **Supports:** aluminum rings or clamps holding the boards (as discussed with
  Thomas), on insulating posts to an aluminum base plate.
  - Posts: PEEK (rigid) or PTFE (best surface resistivity, but creeps). Both
    absorb little moisture.
  - Avoid fiber-filled laminates (G-10/FR-4) with exposed cut edges, per
    Hamish's surface-leakage concern.
  - Rib or undercut the posts for creepage length.
  - Shipping: removable foam blocks that come out before operation.
- **Heat sink:** the "heat sink at the top" idea from the earlier notes is not
  needed. With heating-only control, the insulation sets the loss. A heat sink
  only raises the required heater power.

### Heater circuit wiring (inside)

```text
DB-HTR pin 1 (HTR+) ─ TF1 thermal fuse 72 °C ─ TS1 thermostat NC 49 °C ─ H1 10 Ω ─ H2 10 Ω ─ DB-HTR pin 2 (HTR−)
```

- Use 18 AWG wire with PTFE or silicone insulation, twisted pair, routed along
  the back wall and away from the readouts.
- Expected resistance between DB-HTR pins 1 and 2 at room temperature: ~20 Ω.
- Insulation resistance from the heater circuit to the chassis: > 100 MΩ.

### HV clearance items (for the clearance review)

- The spreader plate, the heater, S1/S2 probe sheaths and the base plate are
  grounded or low-voltage objects inside the box. Include them in the
  clearance and creepage review, especially near the HV-in end.
- Keep S1 and S2 out of the region near the HV end of the stack, or confirm
  the clearance.

## 4. Raspberry Pi header: what every used pin does

The PT100s are not read through "four pins" each. All four MAX31865 boards share
the three SPI data pins, and each board has its own chip-select (CS) pin. The
Pi tells a board "you're next" by pulling its CS low. So the four sensors use
3 shared + 4 CS = 7 pins.

The Pi also has **no analog output pin**. The heater command goes out
digitally on the two I²C pins to the MCP4725 DAC, which produces the analog
0–3.3 V for the driver. One GPIO (17) switches the enable relay.

| Physical pin | Name | Direction | Function | Connects to |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3V3 | power out | 3.3 V for sensor boards | MAX31865 Vin ×4, MCP4725 VDD, INA260 VCC, level-shifter LV |
| 2 | 5V | power | 5 V (input from DC-DC if powered via header; see §5) | relay K1 +, level-shifter HV, LCD VCC |
| 3 | GPIO2 / SDA | I²C data | Bus to DAC, INA260, LCD | MCP4725 SDA, INA260 SDA, level-shifter LV1 |
| 5 | GPIO3 / SCL | I²C clock | same bus | MCP4725 SCL, INA260 SCL, level-shifter LV2 |
| 6, 9, 14, 20, 25 | GND | — | Logic ground | all module GND pins; one wire to driver AGND (star) |
| 11 | GPIO17 | out | **Heater enable**. HIGH = relay closed. Low at boot and on fault or stop. | relay K1 Signal |
| 19 | GPIO10 / MOSI | out | SPI data Pi→sensor boards (shared) | MAX31865 SDI ×4 |
| 21 | GPIO9 / MISO | in | SPI data sensor boards→Pi (shared) | MAX31865 SDO ×4 |
| 23 | GPIO11 / SCLK | out | SPI clock (shared) | MAX31865 SCK ×4 |
| 29 | GPIO5 | out | CS for S1 `control_air` | MAX31865 #1 CS |
| 31 | GPIO6 | out | CS for S2 `monitor_air` | MAX31865 #2 CS |
| 33 | GPIO13 | out | CS for S3 `ground_board` | MAX31865 #3 CS |
| 35 | GPIO19 | out | CS for S4 `spare` (heater plate) | MAX31865 #4 CS |
| 13 | GPIO27 | out | Fan enable: **not fitted** | — |
| 15 | GPIO22 | in | Fan tachometer: **not fitted** | — |
| 24, 26 | GPIO8/7 (CE0/CE1) | — | Hardware SPI chip-selects: **leave unconnected** (the code uses GPIO CS) | — |

These match the defaults in `config.toml` (`D5`, `D6`, `D13`, `D19`,
`output_enable_gpio = 17`).

I²C addresses on the shared bus:

| Device | Address |
|---|---|
| LCD (PCF8574) | 0x27 (or 0x3F) |
| INA260 | 0x40 |
| SHT31-D (optional) | 0x44 |
| MCP4725 (Adafruit) | 0x62 |

## 5. Module-by-module connections

### MAX31865 boards (×4, Adafruit #3328), in the controller box

| Board pin | Connect to |
|---|---|
| Vin | Pi 3V3 (pin 1) |
| GND | Pi GND |
| SCK | Pi pin 23 (shared) |
| SDI | Pi pin 19 (shared) |
| SDO | Pi pin 21 (shared) |
| CS | Pi pin 29 / 31 / 33 / 35 for boards #1 / #2 / #3 / #4 |
| RDY, 3Vo | not connected |
| Jumpers | **Leave as shipped.** 4-wire is the default. |
| **F+ and RTD+** (one terminal block) | the two leads from **one end** of the PT100 (via CB-RTDn pins 1 and 2) |
| **RTD− and F−** (other terminal block) | the two leads from the **other end** (via CB-RTDn pins 3 and 4) |

"F" (force) leads carry the excitation current. "RTD" (sense) leads measure the
voltage, so lead resistance cancels. To identify a PT100's leads, the two
leads that read ~0–2 Ω to each other belong to the same end. The two ends read
about 110 Ω apart at room temperature.

### MCP4725 DAC (Adafruit #935)

| Pin | Connect to |
|---|---|
| VDD | 3V3 |
| GND | GND |
| SDA, SCL | I²C bus |
| A0 | not connected (address 0x62) |
| **VOUT** | driver **TB2-1 CMD**. Run it as a twisted pair with GND → TB2-2 AGND. |

### INA260 (Adafruit #4226)

| Pin | Connect to |
|---|---|
| VCC | 3V3 |
| GND | GND |
| SDA, SCL | I²C bus |
| Alert | not connected |
| Vin+ | relay K1 **NO** |
| Vin− | **CB-HTR pin 1** (HTR+) |
| VBus | leave at the board default (bus voltage sensed at Vin−; confirm in the Adafruit guide) |

### Relay K1 (Adafruit #4409, normally open)

| Pin | Connect to |
|---|---|
| + | Pi 5V |
| − | GND |
| Signal | Pi pin 11 (GPIO17) |
| COM | +24 V after **F2 (1.6 A)** |
| NO | INA260 Vin+ |
| NC | not connected |

### LCD (PCF8574 backpack) through the level shifter (SparkFun BOB-12009)

| Shifter pin | Connect to |
|---|---|
| LV | 3V3 |
| HV | 5V |
| GND (both sides) | GND |
| LV1 / LV2 | Pi SDA / SCL |
| HV1 / HV2 | LCD SDA / SCL |

The LCD's VCC goes to 5V and its GND to GND.

### Linear current driver board

The schematic is in `HEATER_AND_CURRENT_DRIVER.md` §3.

| Terminal | Signal | Connect to |
|---|---|---|
| TB1-1 | +24 V | after F1 (3 A input fuse). Feeds the L7812 → 12 V op-amp supply. |
| TB1-2 | PGND | 24 V return. **This is the star ground point** (bottom of RS). |
| TB2-1 | CMD | MCP4725 VOUT |
| TB2-2 | AGND | MCP4725 GND (this is the only Pi-ground ↔ power-ground tie) |
| TB3-1 | HTR_RETURN (Q1 drain) | CB-HTR pin 2 (HTR−) |

### 24 V input and the 5 V supply for the Pi

```text
CB-PWR (+24 V) ─ F1 3 A T ─┬─ DDR-30G-5 +Vin
                           ├─ driver TB1-1
                           └─ F2 1.6 A T ─ relay K1 COM
CB-PWR (0 V) ──────────────┴─ DDR-30G-5 −Vin, driver TB1-2 (star)
DDR-30G-5 +Vout / −Vout ──► Pi 5 V / GND
```

For the Pi's 5 V, prefer a USB-C pigtail into the Pi's power input. Feeding
the header 5 V pins bypasses the Pi's input protection. The DC-DC is isolated,
so the Pi's ground ties to power ground only through TB2-2. That makes one star
point and no ground loop.

## 6. Cables and connectors between the boxes

| Cable | Controller box | Divider box | Conductors | Pinout |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Heater | CB-HTR | DB-HTR | 2 × 18 AWG twisted (optional overall shield) | 1 = HTR+ (from INA260 Vin−), 2 = HTR− (to driver TB3-1) |
| PT100 #1–#4 (one cable each) | CB-RTD1..4 | DB-RTD1..4 | Belden 8723 (2 individually shielded pairs) | Pair A: pin 1 F+, pin 4 F−. Pair B: pin 2 RTD+, pin 3 RTD−. |
| Protective earth | PE stud | PE stud | ≥ 14 AWG green/yellow | chassis to chassis, and to building PE |
| 24 V in | CB-PWR | — | from the 24 V supply | + / 0 V |
| Network | Pi Ethernet | — | Cat5e/6 | logging, SSH |

- **Pairing:** twist each force pair together and each sense pair together.
  That keeps the excitation and sense loops small.
- **Shields:** connect the PT100 shields at the controller box only (MAX31865
  GND). Cut back and insulate them at the divider box. The final choice belongs
  to the grounding plan.
- **Connectors:**
  - Use a different connector type or keying for the heater than for the
    sensors, so they can't be swapped.
  - Put all of them on the LV/readout side of the divider box, away from HV
    in.
  - Connector family is still open (LEMO per Thomas, or M12 4-pin A-coded):
    TODO **D5**.

---

## 7. Grounding

- **Divider box:** bond all panels with straps (the powder-coated Hammond
  panels are not bonded through their screws) to one PE stud. Check that each
  bond measures < 0.1 Ω.
- **Controller box:** chassis to PE.
- **Electronics:** Pi, MAX31865, DAC, INA260 and driver share one star ground
  at driver TB1-2. Connect it to PE at one point in the controller box.
- **Heater circuit:** insulated from the divider-box chassis. Its only
  connection is the heater cable.
- **Divider readout:** its LV grounding follows the readout plan (LEMO, Thomas).
  Settle that before final cable shield terminations.

## 8. Software mapping for this layout

```toml
[hardware]
mode = "dac"
control_rtd_cs_pin = "D5"        # S1 air, PID input
use_monitor_air_rtd = true
monitor_air_rtd_cs_pin = "D6"    # S2 air, far side
use_ground_board_rtd = true
ground_board_rtd_cs_pin = "D13"  # S3 ground board
use_spare_rtd = true
spare_rtd_cs_pin = "D19"         # S4 heater plate
output_enable_gpio = 17
dac_i2c_address = 0x62
current_driver_full_scale_a = 1.32

[control]
heater_resistance_ohm = 20.0     # measure 4-wire through DB-HTR
max_power_w = 22.0
max_current_a = 1.05
overtemperature_c = 31.0         # applies to S1 always
# INTERIM until TODO S1 adds a per-sensor limit for the heater plate:
trip_on_monitor_overtemperature = false   # S2-S4 warn only; TS1/TF1 protect the plate
```

With `trip_on_monitor_overtemperature = false`, a hot board or heater plate is
logged and shown but does not stop the heater in software. The hardware
thermostat (49 °C) and the thermal fuse (72 °C) still protect it. That is
acceptable for supervised commissioning. Implement TODO S1 before unattended
operation.

The `air PT100 disagreement` warning compares S1 and S2. Its 0.20 °C threshold
will flag real gradients, which is useful data during commissioning.
